reference.source: Miller's Review of Orthopaedics / Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: A congenital variant in which the meniscus (almost always lateral) is abnormally thick and disc-shaped rather than semilunar
Classified (Watanabe) into complete, incomplete and Wrisberg types by coverage and peripheral attachment
Often asymptomatic, but the abnormal shape and sometimes deficient posterior attachment predispose to tears and mechanical symptoms
The classic presentation is a painless snapping or clunking knee in a child (the 'snapping knee syndrome')
Symptomatic tears cause pain, effusion, locking and loss of full extension
MRI shows a bow-tie sign on multiple contiguous sagittal slices and increased meniscal width on coronal images
Asymptomatic discoid menisci need no treatment; symptomatic ones are managed with arthroscopic saucerisation preserving a peripheral rim
reference.pathophysiology: During development the lateral meniscus fails to attain its normal semilunar form, remaining a thickened disc that covers more of the tibial plateau. The thickened, sometimes hypermobile tissue (particularly the Wrisberg variant lacking a stable posterior attachment) is subject to abnormal shear, predisposing to tears and to snapping as it displaces during knee motion. Preserving a peripheral rim during saucerisation maintains meniscal load-sharing function.
additionalDifferentials: Meniscal tear of a normal meniscus
Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral condyle
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the knee (bow-tie sign and increased meniscal width)
Weight-bearing radiographs to assess joint space and exclude other pathology
Arthroscopy for definitive assessment and treatment
Contralateral imaging as the variant can be bilateral
redFlags: A locked knee from a displaced discoid meniscal tear
Progressive effusion and pain limiting function in a child
Signs suggesting osteochondritis dissecans or loose body
reference.prognosis: Asymptomatic discoid menisci have an excellent outlook; symptomatic tears do well after rim-preserving saucerisation, whereas extensive meniscectomy risks early lateral compartment osteoarthritis.
pitfalls: Performing total meniscectomy rather than rim-preserving saucerisation
Missing the diagnosis in a child with painless knee snapping
Overlooking a Wrisberg variant with an unstable posterior horn
Attributing symptoms to the discoid meniscus when osteochondritis dissecans coexists
management: Observation without surgery for asymptomatic, incidentally discovered discoid menisci
Arthroscopic saucerisation, reshaping the disc to a near-normal contour while preserving a peripheral rim, for symptomatic tears or mechanical symptoms
Arthroscopic repair or stabilisation of a deficient posterior peripheral attachment, particularly in the Wrisberg variant
Avoid total meniscectomy because of the risk of early lateral compartment osteoarthritis
Long-term follow-up for lateral compartment osteoarthritis, with assessment of the contralateral knee as the variant can be bilateral
